tagline.text: Mindanao's first World Heritage site, with a century-old bonsai forest

location.label: Location
location.text: San Isidro, Mati & Governor Generoso, Davao Oriental

children.text: A mountain rising to about 1,620m on the Pujada Peninsula in Davao Oriental, made Mindanao's first UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014 thanks to the Philippines' largest pygmy forest, where trees over a hundred years old grow only knee-high. It can only be climbed on a guided trek with prior permission.
Mount Hamiguitan is the highest peak of the mountain range running north-south through the Pujada Peninsula in Davao Oriental, at the southeastern tip of Mindanao, standing about
above sea level. The roughly 6,800 hectares around the mountain form the Mount Hamiguitan Range Wildlife Sanctuary, protected by law in
and, in
, inscribed as Mindanao's first UNESCO World Heritage site. The mountain spans three municipalities: Mati City, San Isidro, and Governor Generoso.
What makes this mountain special is its
pygmy forest (bonsai forest)

. Ultramafic soil rich in iron and magnesium but poor in nutrients, combined with strong wind and thick fog, keeps the trees from growing large, so even trees over a hundred years old stand only 1–1.5m tall, twisted like bonsai. This is the largest such pygmy forest in the Philippines, spanning hundreds of hectares. The forest changes character clearly with elevation, from lowland rainforest at the base to mossy cloud forest and, finally, the pygmy forest.

Biodiversity is remarkable too: endangered species such as the Philippine eagle and Philippine cockatoo live here, and endemic plants and orchids grow throughout, including the pitcher plant Nepenthes peltata, found only on this mountain. Up the mountain there are also sights such as Tinagong Dagat ("hidden sea"), a mysterious bog lake said to rise and fall like a tide, along with Hidden Garden and Twin Falls.

Prior permission from the Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) and an accredited guide are required, and visitor numbers are limited, so this isn't a mountain you can show up to and climb on a whim. In exchange, the forest stays remarkably well preserved, making for an unforgettable experience for hikers seeking ecological trekking beyond the usual mountain trails. Travelers who find the climb daunting can get an indirect taste of the mountain's ecology at the Hamiguitan World Heritage Park at the foot of the mountain in San Isidro.

The pygmy forest, an endless stretch of twisted trees knee- to waist-high, is the highlight of the Hamiguitan trek. Every single tree has grown for over a century fighting the wind, so stay on the designated trail.
On a clear day near the summit, Davao Gulf opens up on one side and the Pacific and Pujada Bay on the other. Time your visit for the brief morning window when the fog clears.
A bog lake hidden in the mossy forest up the mountain, said to rise and fall like a tide. The ground around it is muddy, so follow your guide's path in carefully.
You'll spot several species of pitcher plant, including Nepenthes peltata, found only on this mountain, along with wild orchids throughout the trail. Touching or picking them is prohibited.
Hidden Garden, blanketed in moss and ferns, and Twin Falls, a narrow, tall waterfall near the pygmy forest, are highlights visited on a side trek on the second day.
Spend the night at a camp above roughly 1,100m and you'll experience mist, cool wind, and a sky full of stars. The camp has a water supply drawn from a spring.

A park built in the buffer zone in San Isidro, with a natural history exhibit hall, a bird-watching deck, a hanging bridge, and forest trails, letting family travelers who aren't climbing still experience Hamiguitan's nature.

To climb, you must apply for a permit from the Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) at least
10 days
in advance, or 2–4 weeks ahead to be safe. You'll need ID and a health certificate issued by a local health center, and walk-in visits aren't accepted.
The
San Isidro trail

(starting from Barangay La Union) currently operates year-round, while the Governor Generoso trail is reportedly by special reservation only, and the Mati trail is said to be closed. Which trails are open and any rest-period schedules change often, so check the latest notices.
Hamiguitan sits somewhat outside the main typhoon path, but as a mountain cloud forest it sees frequent rain and fog year-round.
November–February
, when the northeast monsoon blows in off the Pacific, brings the heaviest rain, turning trails muddy and swelling valley streams, so it's best avoided.
March–September
, with relatively less rain, and especially
March–May
, is the best time to climb.

Before and after the climb, stay at a small inn or homestay in San Isidro (about
a night), or a hotel in Mati town, which has more options (about

). Dahican Beach in Mati also has resorts and surfer accommodation, and resting there for a day after the climb is a popular add-on. On the mountain, you camp in tents, bringing your own tent, sleeping bag, and cooking gear, or renting them through a guide outfitter.

There are no shops on the mountain, so you need to bring all the food for the 3 days and 2 nights, and most climbers plan meals of rice, canned goods, and dried food with their porter. The protected area encourages reducing single-use plastic, so bring reusable containers. After descending, be sure to try grilled fish fresh from Pujada Bay, kinilaw (raw fish cured in vinegar), and coconut dishes in Mati, reflecting the region's abundance of coconuts.
Start your permit application at least
10 days
in advance, or about a month ahead in peak season. Visitor limits mean your preferred date can fill up quickly.
For a first visit, the easiest option is a local accredited tour operator who handles the permit, guide, and transport all at once.
The cloud forest section is wet almost all the time. Bring waterproof hiking boots, gaiters, a raincoat, and spare clothes packed in a dry bag.
Nights are chilly, so you'll need a warm jacket and sleeping bag. Pack too lightly based on the coastal temperature and you'll shiver all night.
Some sections have leeches. Bring long socks, insect repellent, and salt or a leech deterrent.
Cell signal is weak on most of the mountain and trail. Before you set out, tell your family your itinerary and your guide's contact number.

If climbing isn't for you, an alternative is visiting the Hamiguitan World Heritage Park in San Isidro and the Subangan Museum in Mati, which introduces the natural history and culture of Davao Oriental.

Hamiguitan is a protected area you cannot enter without a permit. Unauthorized entry, collecting plants or animals, and straying from the designated trail can carry legal penalties, and security conditions in the mountainous areas of Davao Oriental also change from time to time, so be sure to check your home country's latest travel advisories and the management office's notices.
The ultramafic rock and wet dirt trails are very slippery. Use trekking poles, and take extra care of your knees and ankles on the descent.
Valley streams can rise suddenly during heavy rain. If your guide tells you to stop, don't force a crossing.
It's easy to get lost in thick fog. Stay close to your group and guide.
Trees in the pygmy forest take decades to recover once broken. Don't grab branches or step on them.
Carry out all your trash, including food waste. Only build a fire at camp where it's permitted.
